pas:176116.t: Silver 'TOT Roman finger ring: side view
pas:176116.d: A Roman silver finger-ring of Henig's Type XI with plain D-shaped hoop and broad, flat, sub-rectangular bezel. Within a simple channelled border is a rudimentarily incised sub-rectangular panel engraved with the letters ToT, the 'o' being rendered simply as a stop (thus, T.T). pas:246054.t: Roman silver finger ring, inscribed TO.
pas:246054.d: A silver Roman finger ring, Henig Type VIII. The ring bezel is circular and the shoulders are triangular, tapering to an incomplete hoop. The shoulders are decorated with an incised 'V' with perimeter facets to either side. The hoop bears the inscription 'TO',which is an abbreviation for the Celtic god-name Totatis, one of the principal deities in Gaul. Many of these rings are known from the East Midlands, especially in Lincolnshire where the deity appears to have had a large following. The inscription 'TO' is unusual because it is more often rendered ToT or T.T, with the occasional example as TVT. The style of ring is also quite crude when compared to classical Roman rings bearing…

pas:275539.d: The pendant is made of a disc of gold sheet that is scratched and heavily bent in several places. Underneath the now missing loop a triangle is formed by beaded gold wire that is framed by spirals made of thinner beaded wires. Inside the triangle are undecorated gold strips that may have framed a now lost decorative stone. The loop has been cut off. The centre is decorated with the design of an anthropomorphic head with bust in contour lines. In the tradition of the imperial bust on late Roman coins and medallions that served as model the head is shown in profile, the hairstyle is decorated with a diadem, the coat is shown with two brooches and stylized folds, and an inscription in Roman…

pas:282104.t: Fragment of Samien ware dating to the Roman period (45-410AD).
pas:282104.d: Fragment of Samien ware dating to the Roman period (45-410AD). The fragment is from the centre of the base of a vessel. It is circular in plan and D-shaped in profile. The fabric is very hard is light orange in colour and has an orange/red 'satin' gloss slip on both the inner and outer surface. The base is stamped with the inscription CATVSSAM, which is the stamp of the potter CATVSSA. The fragment was produced at Lezoux between 125-140. . In “Roman Samian Pottery in Britain”, Paul Webster (1996) notes that red-slip coated samian ware, made mainly in Gaul and Germany, was imported into Britain from the mid 1st to the mid 3rd centuries

pas:290210.d: A cast copper alloy mount; it is not clear what the mount would have been attached to. The mount is rectangular, flat and now bent over double. At the left hand side of the mount is a wide rectangular panel formed by a perimeter of incised diagonal grooves. This motif is often seen enclosing inscriptions on second and third century finger rings. Within the rectangle is the inscription SALVS. pas:403221.t: Roman coin: contemporary copy of a denarius conflating designs of Julius Caesar and Augustus
pas:403221.d: Roman contemporary (or more recent fantasy) forgery, of a silver denarius, based on obverse portraits of Julius Caesar minted during his lifetime and during the Octavianic/Augustan age and the AEGVPTO (or AEGVPT) CAPTA reverse type of Octavian minted in 28-27 BC. Must therefore post-date 28-27 BC. It appears that this coin is loosely copied from coins of the period. The obverse conflates various elements of coins of Caesar and Octavian/Augustus. The obverse legend D[I]VO IMP has never been employed. It is most likely based on a legend found on a Caesarian coin as well as one on an Octavianic coin: the CAESAR IMP obverse type of Caesar minted in January-February 44 BC (RRC 480/3) and the…

pas:435286.d: A silver Roman finger ring, Henig Type VIII, of which only the bezel and shoulders survive. The ring bezel is circular and the shoulders are also circular. The hoop is missing. The shoulders are decorated with an incised 'V' with perimeter facets to either side decorated with radiating incised lines. The bezel bears the inscription 'TO', which is an abbreviation for the Celtic god-name Totatis, one of the principal deities in Gaul. Many of these rings are known from the East Midlands, especially in Lincolnshire where the deity appears to have had a large following. The inscription 'TO' is unusual because it is more often rendered ToT or T.T, with the occasional example as TVT. The style of…

pas:437399.d: Fragment of a Roman finger ring made of jet or shale. The hoop is thick, D-shaped in cross-section and only remains as part of one shoulder. The bezel is rectangular and very slightly raised from the hoop.The bezel is decorated with an incised rectangle with a hatched border. The interior of the rectangular, which usually carries an inscription, is blank. The design is one that is often seen in silver Roman finger rings of the second and third centuries that equate to Henig's type XI rings.. Jet jewellery was popular in the Roman period, and one of the main sources was the East coast of Yorkshire, so it is likely that this ring was made locally from material in the region. pas:471160.d: A silver Roman 'TOT' ring dating to the second or third century AD. The ring has a circular bezel bearing the inscription TOT, an abbreviation of the Celtic god-name Toutatis. The shoulders of the ring are triangular and decorated with an incised linear perimeter and two circles in each corner near the bezel. The hoop is oval in plan and a slender D-shape in cross-section. The internal diameter of the hoop measures 17mm x 15mm. The bezel measures 7mm in diameter. Treasure reference number 2011 T750. Silver rings bearing the inscription TOT are well known finds from the East Midlands, especially in Lincolnshire

pas:488242.d: Treasure Item 2012 T107: Complete silver Roman finger ring, Henig Type XI, dating to the 2nd - 3rd century AD. The ring is roughly D-shaped with a broad flat bezel and sub-circular hoop. The bezel, which is sub-rectangular in shape, has bevelled shoulders carrying impressed semi-circular detailing outlined with an incised line. This semi-circular detailing flanks either end of the rectangular bezel and below this the shoulders taper to form the narrowed hoop of the ring. Both the shoulders and hoop, which are undecorated, are plano-convex in section. The bezel is inscribed with the lettering DMT and both above and below this lettering there is worn incised hatching in the form of two…

pas:503143.d: A Roman sandstone tombstone from a cemetery site overlooking and adjacent to a Roman road from which other tombstone fragments are known probably dating to the late 2nd century AD. As regards the date of the tombstone, the three upper entries are for men of the gens Aurelia, which presumably points to enfranchisement of the family in the reign of Marcus Aurelius, perhaps at the completion of military service in an auxiliary unit. It could even be that some of the 5, 500 Sarmatians sent to Britain during the reign of Marcus Aurelius (Dio Cassius History of Rome 72.16, 2), were posted to Old Carlisle, although the known garrison of the fort in the later second century was the Ala Augusta…

pas:520100.t: Roman ToT Ring from Kirton in Lindsey
pas:520100.d: A Roman silver finger-ring with a broad rectangular bezel and triangular shoulders. Simple incised lines emphasize the borders and 'frame' the bezel, within which the letters ToT are engraved, the T's with neatly-formed seriphs. There are signs of wear, most notably on the bezel and at the rear of the hoop. Rings with 'ToT' inscriptions are distinctively Romano-British and concentrated in Lincolnshire. The inscription is regarded as an abbreviation of the Celtic god-name Toutatis/ Totatis, a deity who was often conflated with the Roman god Mars (M. Henig and J. Ogden, Antiquaries Journal 67, 1987, 366-7; A. Daubney, 'The cult of Totatis: evidence for tribal identity in mid Roman Britain',…

pas:522247.d: A copper alloy Roman Aucissa brooch dating from AD 43 - 75. The strip brooch has a head formed by rolling the strip forwards to form a tube for the axis bar. Iron corrosion obscures most of the area (presumably from the axis bar) but the head does not appear to be inscribed "Aucissa" as on the brooches which gave this class their name. Only the head of the hinged copper alloy pin survives. A transverse band of ropework decorates the head, and then the strongly arched bow is fluted. A central ridge decorated with ropework is flanked by a channel on each side, and beyond them is another band of ropework along both edges of the bow. pas:540148.t: Roman ceramic stamped amphora handle dating AD 2nd century
pas:540148.d: A Roman ceramic stamped amphora handle dating AD 2nd century. This handle is from a Dressel 20 amphora which would have been large and globular with cylindrical handles and a prominent beaded or angular rim. The fabric is granular. The handle is stamped with an inscription which reads "C . V . [-]". Fiona Seeley identified this as a Dressel 20 and notes that it would have contained olive oil and was produced in the Baetica region of Spain. Calender (1965 no.506) suggests C . V . [-] may be for C. Valeri Variani. Glynn Davis also found a very similar parallel within the London Archaeological Archive and Research Centre Acc. No. 11295. which is published in Funari (1996:72 no. 247).…

pas:540176.t: Barbarous radiate or imitation billon Antoninianus of Claudius II. Obverse view.
pas:540176.d: A complete, Roman, struck or hammered, copper alloy probable barbarous radiate or imitation billon Antoninianus of Claudius II, struck after his death. Obverse: Radiate bust right with a sharp nose and close cropped beard. Inscription: [IMP CLAV]D[IVS AVG]. Reverse: Altar - consecrated in memory. Inscription: [CONSECRATIO]. Mint name: British by provenance. Die axis: 12 o'clock. The coin is slightly worn - very fine condition. The coin has a rusty brown 'sandy' encrusted surface probably due to the water-logged ground conditions, an irregular flan with a small notch and the reverse is struck a little off centre. The coin is likely to date to 270-273AD. Ref. Coins of England and the UK,…

pas:565174.d: A complete, Roman, struck or hammered, silver denarius of Hadrian (117-138AD). Obverse: Laureate bust right, draped and cuirassed. Inscription: [IMP] CAES.TRAIAN.HADRIAN.AVG [DIVITRA]. Reverse: Fortuna seated holding a rudder but no globe with 'Fortred' in the exergue. Inscription: PM[]TRPCOS. Die axis: 6 o'clock. The coin is in very fine condition with little wear. It has an attractive silver colour with just one spot of dark green verdigris on the obverse and the reverse has a slight weak grey tarnish. This coin dates to 117AD following Trajan's death. Ref. Roman Coins and their Values II, David R. Sear, Spink 2002, page 146 no. 3493 and Roman Silver Coins Vol. II, 3rd Edition 1979, page…

pas:565193.d: A complete cast copper alloy barrel shaped weight of Roman/Early Byzantine date (AD 200-450). Other examples are known to have silver guilt in the lettering which is absent in this example. The current thinking in terms of dating for such weights places…

pas:565247.t: Nummi or AE4 of the House of Constantine. Obverse view.
pas:565247.d: A complete, Roman, struck or hammered, nummi or AE4, copper coin of The House of Constantine, commemorative issue. Obverse: Laureate and cuirassed bust right. Inscription: Not applicable. Reverse: Two soldiers standing holding two standards. Inscription: [GLORIA EXERCITVS]. Die axis: 12 o'clock. The coin is in very fine, slightly worn condition but the flan is too small for the die and all the legend is missing. There is some pale green surface corrosion which goes around the slightly irregular edges. There also appears to be the remains of a silvery surface. This coin is likely to date between 330-335AD. pas:566299.d: A rim sherd of Roman samian ware jar containing graffito on the exterior. While the sherd is undoubtedly of Roman date, the date at which the graffito was added is unclear. The second line begins under the [III] of the first line, and runs horizontally to the right wall. This reads INVI [ ]. The exterior surface is badly scratched with many small grooves, and one large groove runs diagonally across the centre of the face over the first lane, cutting across the [IIII] of the inscription. pas:607827.d: TREASURE CASE 2014 T197: An incomplete Roman silver finger ring dating to the second or third century AD. Only the bezel and part of one shoulder survives. The surviving shoulder of the finger ring is lightly arched and tapers inwards towards the missing hoop - The finger ring was probably D-shaped rather than circular in outline, typical for Roman Finger rings of this period. Due to peripheral wear and damage the shape of the bezel is uncertain but appears to be rounded at the edges and has a square incised outline framing the centre. This square outline contains an incised O at the centre and has faint traces of additional incised lines around this. It is suggested that this ring is an…

pas:621369.d: A probable modern copy of a copper alloy Roman radiate of Allectus dating to the period AD 293-96 (Reece Period 14). Reverse inscription: PROVIDENTIA AVG. Reverse image: Providentia standing left, holding a baton and a cornucopiae, globe at foot. Mint unclear - it migh be S P // (ML?) for London, but this type is very rare for London. It is more likely to be S P // (C) for C Mint which is much more common (cf RIC V, pt 2, p. 561, no. 35). The thickness and cast nature of the coin, indicate that this is a forgery and not contemporary to the Roman period. pas:642156.t: Roman: Incomplete Guiraud type 3g finger ring with inscribed bezel
pas:642156.d: An incomplete silver finger ring of Roman date, probably 3rd Century AD. Around 25% of the finger ring is present, consisting of part of the bezel, a shoulder and the start of the hoop. The bezel was originally rectangular in shape, with a recessed border around the edge. The end part of the inscription is present, consisting of the letters 'MT'. This is probably the end of an dedication to either Mars or Mercury. The hoop was probably keeled. The shoulders have been decorated with seven grooved mouldings, creating a ridged effect. pas:649701.d: A complete copper-alloy finger ring dating to the second or third centuries AD. The hoop is hemispherical in section and very worn suggesting use wear. It extends to slightly expanded shoulders. The bezel is oval in plan and is decorated with a stamped inscription within a lozengiform stamped border which reads 'AVE AMA' - 'Greetings. Love (me).' At Ribchester, a gold ring with the inscription 'AVE MEA VITA' has been found (CIL vii 1306) and a further example with the inscription 'AVE ME' found at Carlisle (JRS Iiii (1963) 163, No. 23). The finger ring is 20.7mm long, 8.5mm wide, 1mm thick and weighs 1.8g

pas:708200.d: An incomplete cast copper alloy enamelled zoomorphic plate brooch in the shape of a sitting cockerel of Roman date (AD 100-250). The brooch is piriform in plan, rounded at the front and slightly pointed at the back with a domed upper surface and hollow concave reverse. The zoomorphic / cockerel features consist of a head which extends from the rounded end and a tail emanating from the pointed end. The head is flat and sub-circular in profile; the comb extends above but is lost due to abrasion; the beak is similarly lost. The eyes (one on either side of the head) are made from a drilled ring-and-dot motif; it is possible that the centre of the eye had a red enamel inlay - now lost. The tail…

pas:783095.d: A silver Roman Republic denarius issued by C Antius C.f. Restio, and dating to 47 BC (Reece Period 1). Obverse shows the jugate heads of the Dei Penates and the reverse inscription reads C.ANTIVS C . F; Hercules walking right holding club and trophy, cloak over left arm. Mint of Rome. RRC 455/2a; Syd. 971. The coin has been countermarked, once on the reverse with a 'C' like symbol, while the obverse has two countermarks; at 3 o'clock a 'D' shaped mark on its side, and in the centre an inverted 'V'. If the coin is rotated to 6 o'clock, the countermarks appear as 'AV'

pas:807339.d: Sheet lead rolled strip of unknown date, possibly a 'Roman curse tablet' (AD 43-410), as Roman coins were found in the same field. Although this object has been classified as a curse tablet, it is possibly more modern and may have performed an entirely different function, such as a weight or ingot. The strip has a spiral profile suggesting it was rolled rather than folded, which is more typical of such tablets. Linear ridges may have been created when it was being rolled or they may have taken on an impression of what is within or what the rolled strip was inserted into. pas:841970.d: A fragment of a copper alloy Roman timepiece, AD.100-400. The piece is sub-rectangular strip of copper alloy with a series of perforations running approximately 4mm from the edge of the strip. Write above the line of holes is the word AVGVST in Roman serifed capitals. Below the perforations are the letters N and [I]D. The ends of the piece are damaged and torn with jagged but worn, old breaks. This piece has been shown to John Pearce who states the following. "The N is an abbreviated reference to the Nonae (nones) and what looks like a D alone is presumably ID (traces of I before, perhaps?), i.e, the Idus or ides. A similar fragment was excavated at Vindolanda in 2008, showing part of the…

pas:935647.d: Gold Roman finger ring with inscribed bezel (c. AD 43 - 200). The finger ring has a rectangular-sectioned hoop which widens from a very narrow point to a flat, rectangular bezel. The bezel appears to have been stamped with a rectangular stamp (the outline of which is faintly visible). Incised onto the bezel within the rectangular outline are three initials: G B R. The letters are of unequal size and uncertain execution. The finger ring has been flattened, probably while in the ground, and this has resulted in some fracturing of the hoop at the point where it has been bent. pas:972153.t: Illustration of inscription from Roman Pig Ingot c. 63-69AD (Drawn by S D White)
pas:972153.d: Roman lead pig ingot c63-69AD. The ingot is rectangular in plan and trapezoid in section. Max length: 530mm tapering to 490mm; max width: 160mm tapering to 80mm; height: 110mm tapering to 90mm; weight: 63.4kg. Four clear layers can be seen giving an indication of the way in which the ingot was produced, by pouring four separate batches of metal in the mould. One end of the ingot has been lost and there are cut marks on all faces the ingot. Initial identification is thanks to Sam Moorhead, John Pearce, Roger Tomlin and Mark Lewis. The pig appears to be unique and has an inscription made up of ligatured letters which refer to one of the governors of Roman Britain, Marcus Trebellius Maximus…

pas:NMS-A6F891.d: Circumstances of discovery : The 'near Cookley' hoard was discovered on the 19th of August 2018 by Mr [name redacted], metal detecting on a cultivated field with the landowner's permission. He initially discovered 12 silver denarii, and on returning to the field the next day dug out another 48 from some depth- apparently around 18 inches. The initial finds were spread 'a few yards', but those recovered deeper appear to have been unfortunately dug out of an archaeological context. No pottery sherds were observed by the finder, and thus it seems probable that the coins were buried in an organic container that had since disintegrated. The closely packed nature of the coins is demonstrable by…
